newsitem.title: USA: Group sues CIA to disclose spy spending sum.
newsitem.headline: Group sues CIA to disclose spy spending sum.

text.p: A research group has sued the CIA to compel official disclosure of how much the United States spends on espionage.
In a lawsuit filed Monday, the Federation of American Scientists, founded in 1945 to study national security policy, sought release of the current total under the Freedom of Information Act.
The suit noted that President Bill Clinton had authorised Congress in April 1996 to make public the bottom line for intelligence spending to "promote openness."
Despite the green light for Congress to release the figure, is has not done so, partly out of a conviction that Clinton was trying to duck what could be a controversial move.

"I believe this is starting down a slippery slope," Larry Combest, a Texas Republican who was then chairman of the House Intelligence Committee said on the House floor on May 22, 1996. "I think he is looking for congressional cover."
At issue was the so-called "black budget," the sum earmarked each year by Congress to run the Central Intelligence Agency and its 12 sister spy outfits.

The sum has been authoritatively reported in recent years to total $28 billion to $30 billion a year. In 1994, a congressional panel inadvertantly published a breakdown of much of what was then $28 billion or so in spending.

"Budget secrecy today illustrates both the corruption of CIA information policy and the inadequacy of congressional oversight," said Steven Aftergood, head of the Federation of American Scientists' project on government secrecy.

Aftergood, who filed the suit for the federation, said in an interview that the White House and Congress had been in collusion on the issue and his group was determined to shake the number loose by filing its action.
The CIA declined comment on the suit. The White House did not immediately return a phone call about the matter.

Declaring that official disclosure of the intelligence budget was long overdue, Representative John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat, introduced a bill in February that would make public total appropriations for the current fiscal year and the total amount sought by the administration for the new fiscal year.
As of Tuesday, a total of 80 other members of the House from both parties had backed the bill as co-sponsors, according to Carl LeVan, an aide to Conyers.
"Thirty billion is an awful lot to be authorising and appropriating without an informed public discussion," LeVan said.
